F. Failure to adequately consider reasonable alternatives to the proposed action.
Section 102(2)(c)(iii) of NEPA requires that all agencies of the Federal Government include in all proposals for action a detailed statement of "... (iii) alternatives to the proposed action." This is a substantial requirement, as stated in the Council on Environmental Quality memorandum on improving agency NEPA procedures:
Recommendation #2: Wherever adverse environmental effects are found to be involved in the proposed action, the impact statement should indicate what other interests and considerations of Federal policy might be found to justify those effects. The statement should also indicate the extent to which these stated countervailing benefits could be realized by following reasonable alternatives to the proposed action that would avoid some or all of the adverse environmental effects.
The draft statement's brief discussion of alternatives fails to meet the requirement of substantial analysis for two reasons:

First, there is no consideration of activities which offer substantially the same benefits as ORV use but are less damaging to the environment; and second, there is inadequate consideration of the whole range of possible Departmental restrictions on ORV use which would allow a substantial amount of use without destroying environmental values.
1. Failure to consider activities which offer substantially the same benefits as ORV use but which are less damaging to the environment.
The draft impact statement points out a great many benefits associated with ORV use. Among them are the economic gains enjoyed by ORV manufacturers and dealers, the thrills of racing and speeding across open country, and the sense of family and social unity
